title: CTC Decoding Across Image Windows
summary: How Mirage reads long text lines with a fixed-width reader, keeps context at crop boundaries and preserves repeated letters when joining predictions.
body_markdown:
Imagine photographing a receipt beside a short label. The letters may be about the same height, but the receipt needs much more horizontal space. If we squeeze both text crops into the same rectangle, the long line becomes cramped. We'd like to keep the letters readable while giving the reader a fixed amount of work at a time.


Mirage does this by preserving the line's aspect ratio and sliding a fixed-width window along it. Neighbouring windows overlap so the reader has context near each join. We keep their central frame predictions, assemble them into one sequence, and then apply CTC collapse to get the text. That last ordering matters for a letter that crosses a window boundary, and for repeated letters such as the two o's in “book”.


The same general idea has been used in speech.[Hugging Face's 2022 account of long-form recognition](https://huggingface.co/blog/asr-chunking) describes overlapping CTC chunks and joining their central predictions before decoding. For Mirage's convolutional image reader, we can work through the geometry explicitly. We'll put the frames on a common ruler, measure how far each one can see, and use that to choose where the windows join.

Pointwise projections, channelwise normalisation, gating and averaging over height leave this horizontal support unchanged.


Near an internal window edge, part of that neighbourhood would fall outside the crop. This gives us a geometric reason to overlap windows and discard their edge predictions. Half of our 96-pixel overlap leaves a 48-pixel margin. The first retained frame after a left trim is centred at column 48, with support starting at column 5. The last retained frame before a right trim is centred at column 268, with support ending at column 311. Both neighbourhoods fit inside the 320-pixel window.


The overlap is therefore large enough for the retained interior frames to see their full local context. Reproducing whole-strip outputs still calls for checks of padding at the true line ends, rounding, quantisation and kernel arithmetic. If we change the reader's receptive field or add a global operation, we also need to revisit this construction.

Deleting matching characters at string boundaries doesn't solve this either. It would erase a real double letter when the blank separating its two runs had already been removed.


The engine joins retained frame IDs first and collapses the resulting path once. An equivalent streaming implementation carries the previous raw frame label across chunks,


```text
previous   =   0
text   =   []
for   frame_ids   in   retained_windows:
for   label   in   frame_ids:
if   label   !=   0   and   label   !=   previous:
text.append(charset[label   -   1  ])
previous   =   label
```


The small but essential detail is that` previous` updates on blanks too. It remembers whether a repeated label continues the same run or starts a new one after a blank. Keep it across windows of the same line, and reset it when moving to another line. That is all the boundary state this greedy collapse needs.


Several frame paths can collapse to the same string. This is worth keeping in mind when interpreting greedy decoding. Mirage collapses the most probable frame path. Finding the most probable string would instead require combining the probability mass of all paths that spell it, which can give a different answer. The engine uses the greedy path without a separate language-model search over OCR strings.

## Checks that catch boundary mistakes


We checked the frame-selection rule for every used width from 1 through 10,000 pixels. Each produced exactly the expected global frame indices, including partial last frames and the transition from one window to two.


We also enumerated paths of up to eight frames over two characters and blank, checking every two-chunk split. Carrying the previous raw label gave the same result as a single collapse for all 63,972 splits. These small cases let us check the seams directly, including repeated letters and blanks. Recognition quality on photographs is a separate measurement.


When you try this on an image, the crop remains a good place to start looking for errors. The reader needs the full text region, enough detail to distinguish the characters, and an alphabet that includes them. Joining windows correctly won't recover a letter cut off by the detector.


In Mirage's[structured perception record](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/structured-perception) , the reader supplies the text attached to a region reference. The language decoder does not need to reproduce every character through its own token stream. The[instance mask head](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/instance-segmentation) uses a similar separation for contours. You can try both in the[Mirage playground](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage#sandbox) or through the[Cactus package](https://github.com/cactus-compute/cactus) .
